definition: Not wanting to do something and holding back before agreeing to it.
example: The reluctant goalie took his place in the net only after the coach asked him a second time.
nuance: Reluctant suggests hesitation that may still give way; reticent specifically means holding back from speaking or sharing feelings.
prompt: A shy student has been asked to give a short speech at the school assembly.
options: The reluctant student agreed to speak only after her teacher promised to sit up front.
The reluctant student signed up the moment the sheet went up and begged for a longer slot.
The reluctant student's speech stuck closely to the assembly's theme of kindness.
The reluctant student had never missed a rehearsal, so the principal trusted her to show up.
reasons: She holds back and needs reassurance before saying yes, which is exactly this kind of hesitation.
Rushing to volunteer and asking for more time shows eagerness, the opposite of holding back.
Staying on topic describes a relevant speech, not a speaker who is hesitant.
A perfect attendance record makes someone reliable; it says nothing about unwillingness.

practice.prompt: A grandfather's family gives him his first smartphone as a birthday gift.
options: Grandpa was so reluctant that he ordered a second phone for himself the very next morning.
Since he already owned a phone, the gift felt reluctant, so he passed it to a neighbor.
The reluctant phone survived a fall onto the kitchen tile without a single scratch.
Though reluctant at first, Grandpa eventually let his granddaughter show him how to send photos.
reasons: Buying another one right away shows enthusiasm, which reverses the meaning.
An extra, unneeded item is redundant; the word describes a person's hesitation, not surplus.
Surviving a drop shows toughness or resilience, not any unwillingness to act.
His early resistance that slowly gives way fits the word's sense of hesitant agreement.
